title: Ready to pan Armstrong, who hit high F and called him Pickles
summary: Russell's band was ready to pan Armstrong, but he dethroned Metcalf with big high notes; Armstrong always gave people nicknames, calling Holmes 'Pickles'.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: That was just like... When Louis come, we was ready to pan Louis! You know? See, that's why... Somebody asked me once, didn't I get a big thrill when I found out I was going to be working with Louis Armstrong. I said, "Big thrill for what? We was gettin' ready to pan him!" We was gettin' ready to just let him make one little slip or something, and it would have been all over Louis, you know! No, it wasn't no thrill for us to work with him. We were looking for him to do something wrong!

But he come through. And the only thing Teddy Hill could do was grab Metcalf's crown, and tear it up! Throw it out in the audience. Yeah, that's all Teddy Hill could do. He grabbed that crown, and... Metcalf with his crown. He was King of the Savoy. Yeah, he wasn't the King no more.
Then Louis started hitting them high notes, ending up on high F and one thing or another. Boy, the people were screaming, one-thing-and-another... Boy, everybody in amazement, you know.

Because I mean, other trumpet players would hit them notes, just like they do nowadays. They'd be hitting high notes, but they sound like a flute up there or something. But Louis wasn't playing them like that. Louis was hittin' them notes right on the head, and expanding. They would be notes. He was hittin' notes. He wasn't squeakin'. They wasn't no squeaks. They were notes. Big, broad notes. And nobody had never heard no trumpet player like that before. Yeah, he was great that way. Yes, he was.
People were screamin' and carryin' on. And he hit high F just as loud as he'd hit medium F. Hit 'em all. Play 'em all. "Play the bad ones like you play the good ones. Play 'em loud!"

He had some funny expressions, though. He'd keep you laughing. Boy, he said some funny things. And he would never call nobody by their name. He always had a name for everybody. He called me Pickles. Of course, that wasn't his name for me. I mean, I had that name before I knew him. But he had heard somebody else call me Pickles. "Pickles. Pickles. Yeah, I like that name. Pickles!"
